title: 🏛️ Exams 2006–2026 · present perfect or simple past in exam texts ⭐⭐

questions.prompt: (Exam 2024, general) At the age of 60, John Duffy started volunteering with a health centre in Ottawa, and he still volunteers today. Which form completes the sentence? "Ever since John started volunteering, he ___ a lot of things: driving old people to medical appointments, helping them pick up groceries…"
questions.explanation: "Ever since" joins a starting point in the past to now, and John is still volunteering: the present perfect, has + past participle, has done. "did" and "was doing" are past forms that treat the period as finished; "is doing" says what happens at this moment and ignores the starting point.

questions.prompt: (Exam 2026, technical) A text tells the career of Drew Mascotti, a welder who started working more than 18 years ago and still works. Which word completes the sentence? "For the past 18 years, he has ___ a welder."
questions.explanation: After has, a past participle is needed, and a job is something a person is: the participle of be is been. "worked" is a participle too, but the wrong verb: "worked a welder" does not say what his job is; "learn" and "being" are the base form and the -ing form, which cannot follow has.

questions.prompt: (Exam 2018, general) A text about Earth Day says that people no longer notice how precious our planet is. Which form completes the sentence? "It seems we have ___ what a beautiful gift planet Earth is."
questions.explanation: After have, the verb takes its past participle. The three forms of this irregular verb are forget, forgot, forgotten, and the participle is the last one. "forgot" is the simple past, which does not follow have; "forget" and "forgetting" are the base form and the -ing form.

questions.prompt: (Exam 2017, technical) Tina is a carpenter who trained as an apprentice, and she still works in the trade. Which word completes the sentence? "She ___ worked for residential contractors and on large construction projects."
questions.explanation: Here "worked" is a past participle, so it follows has or have. "She" is one person, so the auxiliary is has. "have" does not agree with a singular subject; "does worked" marks the tense twice, because after does the verb stays in its base form; "is worked" does not make sense.

questions.prompt: (Exam 2016, technical) Tom has problems with his ears, and his friends are helpful. Which form completes the sentence? "They have ___ some signs to communicate with him."
questions.explanation: After have, the past participle is used. The verb is regular, so its participle ends in -ed: learned. "learn" is the base form, "learning" the -ing form and "learns" the form with -s: none of them can follow have.

questions.prompt: (Exam 2013, technical) Jim is a painter. He is not working today, because yesterday he could not remember where his ladder was. Which form completes the sentence? "He isn't working today because he hasn't ___ his ladder."
questions.explanation: hasn't is has + not, so it is followed by a past participle. Get is irregular: get, got, got. "getting" is the -ing form and "gets" the form with -s, which cannot follow hasn't; "getted" adds -ed to an irregular verb.

questions.prompt: (Exam 2012, general) Tony is a 15-year-old school boy, and he still does voluntary work today. Which form completes the sentence? "He ___ voluntary work for three years."
questions.explanation: "for three years" gives the length of a period that is not over, since Tony is still a volunteer: present perfect, has + past participle. "have done" does not agree with "He"; "does" and "is doing" are present forms that ignore the three years.

questions.prompt: (Exam 2006) Dave and Jenny have known each other for many years, and they still live next to each other. Which form completes the sentence? "They ___ neighbours since they were children."
questions.explanation: "since they were children" starts a period that goes up to now, because they are still neighbours: present perfect, have been. "were" is a simple past that treats the period as finished; "has been" uses a singular auxiliary with "They"; "have being" puts the -ing form after have, where a past participle is needed.

questions.prompt: (Exam 2020, general) A woman remembers her mother, who took pictures as a hobby when the family lived in Mexico, long ago, when she was a little girl. Which form completes the sentence? "She ___ outside the home because she believed that spending time with us was the greatest job of all."
questions.explanation: The story takes place in the writer's childhood in Mexico, a finished period, so the simple past is used. The reason she gives shows that her mother stayed at home: negative, didn't work. "hasn't worked" is a present perfect, which does not go with a finished time; "doesn't work" is a present form; "worked" says the opposite of the reason given.

questions.prompt: (Exam 2010, technical) Diana has always wanted a job in engineering, and she is still trying to get one. Which form completes the sentence? "Since she left school, she ___ letters to all the engineering firms in her home town."
questions.explanation: "Since she left school" gives a starting point in the past, and she has been writing from then until now: the present perfect, has written. "have written" uses a plural auxiliary with "she"; "wrote" is a simple past that closes the period; "writes" is a present form that ignores the starting point.

questions.prompt: (Exam 2009, technical) An apprentice carpenter writes about his work: "I ___ been here for four years now. This company has ___ my life." Which pair completes the two gaps?
questions.explanation: Both gaps are in present perfect forms. After "I", the auxiliary is have (have been), and after has the verb takes its past participle, changed. "has / changed" uses a singular auxiliary with "I"; "have / changing" puts an -ing form after has, where a participle is needed; "has / changing" makes both mistakes.
